doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Gordon Smith and Vic Kirch's band at Thompson's
summary: At 15 or 16 he visits his father's gig and meets Gordon Smith, a great drummer, and Vic Kirch's rhythm and blues band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Who were the musical people in Utica that you kind of looked up to at the time?

Well I started getting out playing pretty early, playing with the older guys that is, the jazz musicians, when I was about 15 or 16. I think I met — well the first guys I met were Gordon Smith, Vic Kirch, and Vic Kirch’s band when he still had the rock & roll band. My mother said, “Well you want to learn about this music you might as well go visit your father.” So I went to one of his gigs at Thompson’s in Whitesboro. And he had Gordon Smith and Billy Grimes playing the bass and my father playing piano. And the place was jammed with all the kids from Proctor High School and Whitesboro Central School and UFA, doing the 50s thing. The early 50s thing.
So they would have been playing—

Vic played music like Fanny Brown, Wynonie Harris, music, of the so-called race music of the early 50s. And the Utica kids ate it up. And I went in and he had this fabulous rhythm section. Gordon Smith was truly a great drummer. And he had lived, he had a heart defect and died Labor Day of 1959. I think he was 28. But if he had lived and had come to New York, which is where he was born, he really was a great drummer. To me his level of accomplishment, artistically, was that of an Arthur Taylor or Philly Joe even. He was distinctive. His style was easily recognizable when you heard him, and he was
fairly unique, not unlike an Elvin Jones or a Philly Joe. And he was pretty wise for his age too. He seemed old to me then, I was 17 then or 16. But he taught me things about life and music as well.
